summary: Updates the guidelines and IANA registration procedures for defining new URI schemes. It obsoletes RFC 4395 and describes how schemes should be documented and registered.

eli5.summary: Rules for inventing new kinds of web-address prefixes like http: and how to put them on the official list.

who reviews iana uri scheme registrations
subtitle: The rules for inventing a new URI scheme such as http: and getting its name onto the official IANA list.

tldr.problem: Anyone can invent a URI scheme, but scheme names share one global namespace, so without clear rules names collide, clash with existing ones, or leak out of private use.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7595 sets design guidelines for scheme definitions and defines three registration statuses (Permanent, Provisional, Historical) in a single IANA registry, with a short template and a Designated Expert for review.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4395, makes Provisional registration First Come First Served, and registers the example scheme for documentation. It has since been updated by RFC 8615.

today: RFC 7595 obsoletes RFC 4395 and has been updated by RFC 8615. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 35).

sections.title: Why a Scheme Registry Exists
sections.content:
Every URI begins with a scheme name, as defined by RFC 3986. The scheme refers to a specification for identifiers within that scheme, which makes the URI syntax a federated and extensible naming system.

RFC 7595 gives updated guidelines for defining new schemes and an updated process for registering them in the IANA URI Schemes registry. There is a single namespace for registered schemes. The registry is meant to give a central point of discovery, discourage multiple uses of the same name, help proposers avoid confusing names, and encourage registration by keeping the barrier low.

It obsoletes RFC 4395, which in turn obsoleted RFC 2717 and RFC 2718. URN namespaces are specific to the urn scheme and are not covered. IRIs use the same scheme names as URIs, so the same registry serves both.
sections.eli5: The first word of a web address needs to be unique, like a team name. The list keeps teams from picking the same name by accident.

sections.title: Requirements for Permanent Schemes
sections.content:
Meeting the guidelines in this section is REQUIRED for Permanent registration, and Permanent status is REQUIRED for schemes defined or normatively referenced by IETF Standards Track documents. A scheme definition cannot override the overall URI syntax, and it must specify the scheme name and the syntax of the scheme-specific part.

  • Utility: new schemes cost effort in clients, gateways, proxies and caches, so the specification SHOULD discuss why the scheme is useful beyond existing ones.
  • Syntax: a scheme MUST define its own scheme-specific syntax, SHOULD reuse the common components of RFC 3986 for hierarchical names, and SHOULD NOT use // unless the scheme-specific part has a hierarchical naming authority.
  • Well defined: it MUST be clear how the scheme functions, and a mapping to another protocol or namespace SHOULD work in both directions.
  • Operations: the scheme SHOULD define applicable operations and a default operation, which SHOULD be safe.
  • Context of use: if the scheme is for specific protocols or applications, say so and reference them.
  • Characters: if URIs carry text, the definition MUST describe the character encoding and be as restrictive as possible.
  • Security and privacy: definitions MUST include a clear analysis.
sections.eli5: If you want your word on the official list forever, you have to explain what it is for, how the addresses are written, and what can go wrong.

sections.title: Choosing a Scheme Name
sections.content:
New scheme names MUST follow the RFC 3986 syntax, which allows only a limited set of US-ASCII characters. The syntax is case insensitive, but the name MUST be registered in lowercase. Names SHOULD be short but descriptive, and SHOULD NOT be very general, grandiose (for example alluding to being "universal" or "standard") or likely to raise trademark problems.

A scheme name is not a protocol, but like a service name from RFC 6335 it often identifies one. If a scheme name corresponds one-to-one with a service name, the two SHOULD be the same.

Organizations that want a private namespace SHOULD use a prefix based on their domain name in reverse order, such as com.example.mything. To protect these, newly registered names MUST NOT contain a . unless they are built from a reversed domain name.
sections.eli5: Pick a short, honest name and do not call yourself "the best". A company can put its own website name backwards in front, like a stamp that says the name is theirs.

sections.title: Provisional, Historical and Private Use
sections.content:
Besides Permanent, there are two other statuses. Provisional registration is for schemes that are not part of a standard but are in use beyond a single organization, or as a step towards Permanent. It needs a valid name, no existing entry with the same name, and contact information. Third parties may register schemes they find in use, in which case both the registrant and the scheme creator SHOULD be identified. If there is no permanent, citable specification, credible reasons SHOULD be given.

Historical registration notes a scheme that is no longer in common use or whose use is not recommended. Any such scheme MAY be designated Historical, and the registration SHOULD say where it was previously documented.

Unregistered schemes cause problems when use leaks out of a single organization, so a unique namespace MUST be used for private schemes, and Provisional registration is strongly encouraged unless the name is built from a domain name.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of entry: forever, for now, and retired. If you are only using a name inside your own club, make it so unusual that nobody else could pick it.

sections.title: How Registration Works
sections.content:
The policy for Provisional registration changed from Expert Review to First Come First Served. Permanent and Historical registration remain Expert Review. A registrant first checks the IANA registry for the name, prepares a registration request using the template, and for Permanent requests sends it to uri-review@ietf.org for review (four weeks is called reasonable) before submitting it to IANA.

IANA checks the request for completeness. A Provisional request with no existing entry is simply added. Otherwise the entry is marked Pending Review and the Designated Expert evaluates it. For Permanent requests the expert may accept, suggest Provisional instead, request IETF review and IESG approval, or ask for more discussion. The IESG is the final arbiter of contested registrations.

The expert's role is to ensure the open review process was followed and to raise concerns about wider implications, not to override IETF or working group consensus. Provisional entries can be updated by the original registrant or their designee, and moving a Permanent entry to Historical requires IESG approval.

The template asks for: scheme name, status, applications or protocols that use the scheme, contact, change controller and references. Fields such as syntax, semantics and security considerations were dropped from the template and now belong in the scheme specification.
sections.eli5: You check the name is free, fill in a short form and send it in. A helper reads it, and for a quick "for now" name the answer is usually just yes if nobody has it yet.

sections.title: The example Scheme
sections.content:
Documentation needs a scheme name that will never clash with a real one. RFC 7595 registers example as a Permanent scheme for that purpose. The whole range of RFC 3986 syntax is allowed, so example:foo, example:/foo and example://foo are all valid.

These URIs are for documentation only. They must not be used as locators, identify any resources, or specify operations, and the scheme MUST NOT be used for any protocol. The change controller is the IETF.
sections.eli5: It is a pretend name for use in books and manuals, like writing "Jane Doe" on a sample form.

sections.title: IANA Changes and Security
sections.content:
IANA merged the former Permanent, Provisional and Historical subregistries into one registry with a Status column (Permanent, Provisional, Historical or Pending Review) and a Notes column that is normally empty. It also added the example scheme and pointed the registry at this document.

On security, all registered values are expected to carry clear security considerations. Because knowledge of vulnerabilities changes over time, new findings may need to be attached to existing documentation so users are not misled about a registered scheme's security properties.
sections.eli5: The three separate lists became one list with a label on each name. And if someone later finds a danger in a name, that warning should be written down next to it.
